'''Imre Gyula Csizmadia''' (October 30, 1932 – July 13, 2022) was a Canadian Hungarian chemist, university professor, external member of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]].

== Early life and education ==
Imre Gyula Csizmadia was born in [[Budapest]] on October 30, 1932. His early studies were determined by Márton Sain, who taught at the Lónyai Street Grammar School in Budapest, and Károly Benkő, a chemistry teacher from [[Szeghalom]] who fled from the [[Royal Hungarian Franz Joseph University]] in Cluj.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.kfki.hu/chemonet/mkf/akademia/csizmadia.html | title=Székfoglaló }}</ref> During his university years at the [[Technical University of Budapest]], he was most influenced by András Messmer, who taught theoretical chemistry at the university. He graduated as a chemical engineer in 1956, but continued his studies in physical organic chemistry at the [[University of British Columbia]] in Canada (M.Sc., 1959, Ph.D., 1962). During his post-doctoral period, he gained experience in quantum chemistry computing at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] and the University Computer Centre in England (NATO Science Fellow, 1962–1964). In 1964, he was appointed Professor at the [[University of Toronto]], where he has been involved in both research and teaching ever since.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://summerabroad.utoronto.ca/index.php/programs/Science/topic/Courses |title=Science - Science Abroad Courses - Summer Abroad Program - University of Toronto |access-date=2012-10-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130729041403/https://summerabroad.utoronto.ca/index.php/programs/Science/topic/Courses |archive-date=2013-07-29 }}</ref>

In 2002, as a [[Szent-Györgyi]] scholarship holder, he spent a short period at [[ELTE]] and then at the [[University of Szeged]] (Hungary). He helped the research and teaching activities of the computational chemistry group led by Béla Viskolcz at the Department of Chemical Informatics ([[University of Szeged|SZTE]]) as an emeritus professor until 2015. By his initiative, a summer school was created within which students from [[SZTE]] and [[University of Toronto]] mastered computational chemistry methods. Between 2015 and 2022, he helped to introduce computational chemistry research at the [[University of Miskolc]].

Since then, he has been a visiting professor in many countries around the world: in Canada, Argentina, Japan, China, England, Germany, France, Spain, Italy and, of course, Hungary. He received honorary doctorate from the [[Eötvös Loránd University]] (1988), [[National University of San Luis]] (Argentina, 2007) and [[Semmelweis University]] (2022).

His main scientific activities are aimed at developing practical theoretical methods for drug design, in which he has already involved second year students.<ref>[https://u-szeged.hu/sztehirek/hirarchivum/2012-majus/bioaktiv-molekulakat Kanadai és európai hallgatókat lát vendégül Szegeden az SZTE Juhász Gyula Pedagógusképző Kar Kémiai Informatika Tanszéke kéthetes Nyári Egyetem programsorozata keretében]</ref> He used more effective, personalised, inspirational teaching techniques (inquiry-based learning/teaching) instead of the conventional so-called information-based teaching of knowledge transfer.

== Career ==
Together with Malcolm C. Harrison, Jules Moskowitz, and Brian Sutcliffe, he carried out the mathematical design of the POLYATOM program package and the development of the software. (POLYATOM<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://rmp.aps.org/abstract/RMP/v35/i3/p571_1 | doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.35.571 | title=Mechanized Molecular Calculations---The POLYATOM System | journal=Reviews of Modern Physics | date=July 1963 | volume=35 | issue=3 | pages=571–572 | last1=Barnett | first1=Michael P. | bibcode=1963RvMP...35..571B | url-access=subscription }}</ref> was the first software package for ab initio calculations using Gaussian orbitals, developed in [[John C. Slater]]'s Solid State and Molecular Theory Group.)

In 1968, he was the first to perform LCAO-MO-SCF ("ab initio") calculations on a formamide molecule using atom-centered Gaussian type (GTF) non-contracted basis functions, determining the ionization potential, dipole moment of the ground state molecule.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Robb |first1=M. A. |last2=Csizmadia |first2=I. G. |title=Non-empirical LCAO-MO-SCF-CI calculations on organic molecules with Gaussian type functions: IV. Preliminary investigations on formamide |journal=Theoretica Chimica Acta |volume=10 |issue=3 |date=1968 |issn=0040-5744 |doi=10.1007/BF00529348 |pages=269–284 |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF00529348 |access-date=2026-08-05|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Later, he studied the theoretical background of the stereochemical consequences of electron pairs and polar bonds in side-by-side positions (Edward-Lemieux, also known as the anomeric effect).<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://pubs.rsc.org/en/Content/ArticleLanding/1971/J2/J29710000136 | doi=10.1039/J29710000136 | title=A theoretical study of the Edward–Lemieux effect (The anomeric effect). The stereochemical requirements of adjacent electron pairs and polar bonds | journal=Journal of the Chemical Society B: Physical Organic | date=January 1971 | pages=136–145 | last1=Wolfe | first1=Saul | last2=Rauk | first2=Arvi | last3=Tel | first3=Luis M. | last4=Csizmadia | first4=I. G. | url-access=subscription }}</ref> He has experimentally investigated the mechanism of [[Wolff rearrangement]], showing that the gas-phase Wolff rearrangement of α-keto carbons occurs via an oxy-oxygen intermediate state.<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja01028a041?journalCode=jacsat&quickLinkVolume=90&quickLinkPage=7360&selectedTab=citation&volume=90 | doi=10.1021/ja01028a041 | title=Mechanism of the Wolff rearrangement | year=1968 | last1=Csizmadia | first1=Imre G. | last2=Font | first2=J. | last3=Strausz | first3=Otto P. | journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume=90 | issue=26 | pages=7360–7361 | bibcode=1968JAChS..90.7360C | url-access=subscription }}</ref> He has demonstrated the thermodynamic and kinetic stability of the oxirene molecule formed during the mechanism by semiempirical (Hückel method) and ab initio calculations.<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00432a016?journalCode=jacsat&quickLinkVolume=98&quickLinkPage=4784&selectedTab=citation&volume=98 | doi=10.1021/ja00432a016 | title=Mechanism of the Wolff rearrangement. 6. Ab initio molecular orbital calculations on the thermodynamic and kinetic stability of the oxirene molecule | year=1976 | last1=Strausz | first1=O. P. | last2=Gosavi | first2=R. K. | last3=Denes | first3=A. S. | last4=Csizmadia | first4=I. G. | journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume=98 | issue=16 | pages=4784–4786 | bibcode=1976JAChS..98.4784S | url-access=subscription }}</ref>
In 1976, using the model compound PH5, he studied Berry pseudorotation (BPR) and turnstile rotation (TR) describing the intramolecular ligand exchange reaction of phosphoranes. Showing that the activation energy of the BPR mechanism is small (1.95 kcal/mol)<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00422a028?journalCode=jacsat&quickLinkVolume=98&quickLinkPage=1450&selectedTab=citation&volume=98 | doi=10.1021/ja00422a028 | title=Intramolecular ligand exchange in phosphoranes. A comparison of Berry pseudorotation and turnstile rotation | year=1976 | last1=Altmann | first1=Julianna A. | last2=Yates | first2=Keith | last3=Csizmadia | first3=I. G. | journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume=98 | issue=6 | pages=1450–1454 | bibcode=1976JAChS..98.1450A | url-access=subscription }}</ref> while for TR it is much higher (10.5 kcal/mol). In 1978, together with M. R. Peterson, he carried out the first ab initio calculations and prepared a potential energy hyperplane for solving the n-butane conformational problems.<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00490a023?journalCode=jacsat&quickLinkVolume=100&quickLinkPage=6911&selectedTab=citation&volume=100 | doi=10.1021/ja00490a023 | title=Analysis of the topological features of the conformational hypersurface of n-butane | year=1978 | last1=Peterson | first1=Michael R. | last2=Csizmadia | first2=Imre G. | journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume=100 | issue=22 | pages=6911–6916 | bibcode=1978JAChS.100.6911P | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 1985, he founded the [[Journal of Molecular Structure: THEOCHEM]], a computational chemistry journal, and served as its editor until 2003 (the journal has been published bi-weekly as [[Computational and Theoretical Chemistry]]<ref>{{Cite web | title=Computational and Theoretical Chemistry - Elsevier | url=http://www.journals.elsevier.com/computational-and-theoretical-chemistry/#description | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111119024114/http://www.journals.elsevier.com:80/computational-and-theoretical-chemistry | access-date=2026-05-22 | archive-date=2011-11-19}}</ref> since 2011).

He was the first President of the [[World Association of Theoretical and Computational Chemists]] ([[WATOC]]) from 1987 to 1990.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.watoc.net/watoc.history.html | title=WATOC - History }}</ref> He organized the first [[WATOC]] conference in [[Budapest]] in 1987 (12–18 August) and the second in [[Toronto]] in 1990. Since then, [[WATOC]] has grown over the years into the largest theoretical and computational chemistry conference, held every three years.

His research interests were mainly in the field of theoretical organic chemistry, with a strong interest in the topology of potential hypersurfaces, mainly investigating the conformational behaviour of oligopeptides. In addition, he was also involved in the study of changes in biomolecules during [[oxidative stress]] and the study of protonation states of ground and excited states.

Till the end of his life, he was an active researcher, author and editor of a large number (550) of scientific publications and 14 books, and according to [[Web of Knowledge]], his total references exceed 13,000, he considered his students to be his most important achievement. He received this guideline or philosophy of life from his mentor [[John C. Slater]] with whom he worked between from 1962 to 1964, and who also valued training the next generation of researchers more than building his own career.

==Interesting facts==
His name appears in the acknowledgement of [[Cube (1997 film)]], a cult film of the late 1990s.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1278988/ |title=Imre G. Csizmadia |website=IMDB}}{{User-generated source|certain=yes|date=August 2022}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
* Fellows of the Chemical Institute of Canada (1970)
* Member of European Academy (1979)
* Honorary Member of the Hungarian Chemical Society (1986)
* Honorary Doctorate, Eötvös Loránd University (1988)
* Honorary Professor at Tianjin Normal University (China) (1988)
* E.W.R. Steacie Award in Chemistry, The Chemical Institute of Canada (1990)
* President of the World Association of Theoretically Oriented Chemists (WATOC)	(1985-1990)
* Angelo Mangini Gold Medal, the Italian Chemical Society (1992)
* Márton Kajtár Medal of the Kajtár Foundation (1999)
* elected External Member of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences (MTA) (2004)
* Honorary Doctorate from the National University of San Luis (Argentina) (2007)
* Honorary Doctorate from Semmelweis University (2012)
